text:
THE COURT OF APPEAL FOR SASKATCHEWAN

Citation: 2008

SKCA 4                                                  Date:
20080114

Between:

Docket:1223

Her Majesty the Queen

Appellant

- and -

David Ahenakew

Respondent

-
and -

The
League for Human Rights of B’nai Brith
Canada

Intervener

Coram:

Lane, Richards & Smith JJ.A.

Counsel:

W. Dean Sinclair for
the Appellant

Douglas H. Christie for
the Respondent

Steven G. Slimovitch for the Intervener

Appeal:

From:
2006 SKQB 272

Heard:               June 21, 2007

Disposition:        Dismissed

Written Reasons: January 14, 2008

By:                   The Honourable Mr. Justice
Richards

In Concurrence:  The Honourable
Mr. Justice Lane

The Honourable Madam Justice Smith

Richards J.A.

I.      Introduction

[
1
]    The respondent, David Ahenakew, spoke
at a conference in 2002.  In the course of his remarks, he made a disparaging comment
about people of the Jewish faith.  After the speech, he was asked for an
interview by a newspaper reporter.  The interview was brief and
confrontational.  Mr. Ahenakew made statements to the reporter which were, in
effect, a rationalization of the Holocaust.

[
2
]    Mr. Ahenakew was charged under
s.
319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
with wilfully promoting hatred.  Following a
trial in the Provincial Court,
he was convicted on the basis of the statements made to the reporter.  He then
appealed to the summary conviction appeal court,
i.e.
the Court of
Queen’s Bench.  The appeal judge quashed the conviction and ordered a new
trial.  He did so on the basis that the trial judge had failed to consider
relevant evidence when determining whether Mr. Ahenakew had the intent
necessary for a finding of guilt.  The Crown takes issue with that decision.

[
3
]    I conclude, for the reasons which
follow, that the Crown’s appeal must be dismissed.  The trial judge did not
take into account all of the evidence bearing on the question of whether Mr.
Ahenakew “wilfully promoted” hatred. As a result, the appeal judge made no
error in ordering a new trial.

II.    Factual Background

[
4
]    On December 13, 2002, the Federation
of Saskatchewan Indian Nations (“FSIN”) sponsored a conference in Saskatoon.  It concerned the imposition by
the Government of Canada of a requirement that aboriginal people sign a consent
form before medical services were supplied by the Government.  The FSIN invited
members of the press to attend.  James Parker, a reporter with the Saskatoon
StarPhoenix
, was assigned
to cover the event.

[
5
]    Two or three hundred delegates were in
attendance.  Conference organizers asked Mr. Ahenakew to make opening remarks.
He spoke for about 45 minutes.  The speech was rambling and disjointed.  It was
not confined to the conference topic. Mr. Ahenakew began by saying this:

Good morning, I ah, I don’t apologize for
being late, I don’t apologize for being alive, I don’t apologize for what I am
and ah I don’t apologize for what I’m going to say to you.  [Continuing in the
Cree language] I welcome all of my relatives and all my relations.  It is good
that we have gotten together to come and listen, and see what we are going to
do.  We have started to look at our Treatys and our Treaty rights.  This person
called a white person will never stand, stand up for you, for anything.  When
he first got here, he started to break our people.  He started to take
everything, he would grab it from us, and then he started to lie and steal from
us. that’s why I call them liars and thieves.  That’s what we have as
neighbours in this country.  [Continuing in English]  Anyway, good morning, and
you can tell by my few words in Cree that ah, I’m pissed off, okay?  I’m, I’m
really angry.

[
6
]    Mr. Ahenakew referred to people of the Jewish
faith toward the end of his speech:

... I always remember when I, when I was in
the armed forces. I ah, after Korea and I, and then I was in Canada for, until 1957 and then I went to Germany for two years with my family. One
of my daughters was born over there, Janet. But ah, the Germans used to tell
me, and I got to know them well because I played soccer against them and with
them and so forth. But they used to tell me that you guys are blessed. What we
know about the Indians in Canada. They are blessed. But that blessing is being destroyed by the, by
your immigrants that are going over there. Especially the Jews, they say, you
know. The Second World War was created by the Jews and the Third World War,
whatever it is, right now, the war that war..., that wages on in Israel, in the Arab countries, I was there
too. But there’s gonna be a war because the Israelis and the “Bushies”, you
know, the bully, the bully, the ah, the bigot and so forth in the United States that tells you that if you’re
not with me, you’re against me. ...

[
7
]    Mr. Ahenakew finished his remarks and sat down.  Some
time later, Mr. Parker approached him for an interview.  Mr. Ahenakew
consented.  He knew Mr. Parker was a reporter and that he wrote columns about
aboriginal affairs for
The StarPhoenix
.  Mr. Ahenakew had sometimes
not agreed with the opinions expressed by Mr. Parker.  Mr. Ahenakew testified
that he assumed the interview would be about the topic of the conference, the
new consent forms introduced by the Government.

[
8
]    Mr. Ahenakew and Mr. Parker moved to the end of a
table to conduct the interview.  Mr. Parker had a tape recorder but Mr.
Ahenakew says he did not see it.  Mr. Parker believes his first question to Mr.
Ahenakew was “You said that your German friends told you the Jews started the
Second World War, do you agree with them?”  For his part, Mr. Ahenakew says Mr.
Parker’s first question was “What the hell do you mean that the Jews started
the Second World War?”  Except for the opening words of Mr. Parker’s initial question,
the entire interview was recorded as follows:

Q         You agree with them.

A         The Jews own damn near owned all of Germany. Prior to the war. That, that’s how
Hitler came in, that he was gonna make damn sure that the Jews didn't take over
Germany or Europe. That’s why
he fried six million of those guys, you know.

Q         Okay. D’you think that it was a good thing that he, that he
killed six million Jews? Isn’t that a horrible thing?

A         Well, Jews, Jews owned the goddamn world and look at what
they're doing. They’re killing people in the Arab countries. I was there, I was
there.

Q         I know, but how can you justify the
holocaust? Six million?

A         You know, how, how do you get rid of a, a, a, you know, a
disease like that that’s gonna take over, that’s gonna dominate, that’s gonna
everything, and the poor people, they ...

Q         How were they taking over Germany? How were they taking over Germany?

A         They owned the banks, they owned the factories, they owned
everything. They loaned money out to the peasants knowing damn well that they
can’t pay it back so they took their land.

Q         Well, how is it that the Germans mounted a war effort
without the Jews because the Jews by that time were gone, because a lot of the
German companies were owned by Germans. And I'm talking about Krupe (phonetic).

A         In name only.

Q         But the Krupe.

A         In name only.

Q         Krupe have made ah, some of the best guns for the German
army, ah, those various chemical companies that were owned by, I mean, the
Germans owned the German economy.

A         Well, I’m not gonna argue with you
about the Jews.

Q         Okay.

A         Or the Germans or anybody else. All I know is that the
Germans told me when I was there two years.

Q         And you believe them.

A         Of course I believe them.

Q         But they, weren’t ...

A         Well, because I saw the Jews kill people in, in the Egypt when I was over there. And the
Palestinians, the Egyptians, the, the Arabs, generally, eh. I saw them fucking
dominate everything.

Q         But wasn’t Canadian army, ah, over in Europe to, to
liberate the Jews, in a sense?

A         No, no, no, to liberate the world,
not the Jews.

Q         To liberate the world (inaudible)
...

A         We didn’t give a damn about the
Jews.

Q         But to liberate the world from a dictatorship that was
killing people, killing Jews, killing gypsies, killing homosexuals, killing all
sorts of people.

A         Exactly. Wanna clean up the world.
I, I don’t support Hitler but I ...

Q         That’s what it sounds like.

A         Well, you know, he cleaned up a hell of a lot of things,
didn’t he? You’d be, you’d be dominated by, you’d be owned by the Jews right
now the world over. Look at a small little country like that and everybody supports
them, the States, who in the hell owns many of the banks in the States, many of
the corporations, many, well, look it here in Canada, ASPER.

Q         Yeah.

A         (Inaudible) ASPER, he controls the
media.

Q         Yeah.

A         Well, what the hell does that tell
you? You know, that’s power.

Q         Well, what does it tell you?

A         That’s fucking power.

Q         What, what, yeah, so he’s a Jewish man that owns a bunch
of newspapers but there are, there are English people, there are (inaudible).
There are non-Jews that own the media companies, there are non-Jews that ...

A         Anyway, anyway, to hell with the
Jews. I can’t stand them and that’s it.

Q         Okay.

A         Don’t talk about them.

Q         Okay.

[
9
]    The interview lasted a total of three minutes.  It
ended at Mr. Ahenakew’s initiative.  He walked away.

[
10
]  Shortly after the interview, Mr. Parker telephoned
Mr. Ahenakew but Mr. Ahenakew hung up on him.

III.
Criminal Code
Provisions

[
11
]

Mr. Ahenakew was charged under
s. 319(2) of the
Code
with wilfully promoting hatred against people of
the Jewish faith in connection both with the statements made during his speech
and the statements made during the subsequent interview with Mr. Parker.  Section
319(2) is set out below:

319
. …

(2) Every one who, by communicating
statements, other than in private conversation, wilfully promotes hatred
against any identifiable group is guilty of

(a) an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment
for a term not exceeding two years; or

(b) an offence punishable on
summary conviction.

IV.   The Trial Judgment

[
12
]  The trial decision is now
reported at
2005 SKPC 76
, (2005), 267 Sask. R. 124.  The trial judge began by
reviewing s. 319(2) and referring to some of the leading cases, such as
R.
v. Keegstra
,
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697, which have interpreted it.  He then
turned to the two sets of comments which were the basis of the charge against
Mr. Ahenakew.

[
13
]  The trial judge dealt first with the comments
Mr. Ahenakew had made during the course of his speech.  While not
believing all of Mr. Ahenakew’s evidence on the issue, he decided not to convict
on the basis of the speech.

[
14
]  The trial judge then turned to the statements made by
Mr. Ahenakew during the interview with Mr. Parker.  In relation to those
statements, Mr. Ahenakew’s primary defence at trial was that the interview
was a “private conversation” and therefore did not fall within the ambit of s.
319(2).  The trial judge rejected this position.  He explained his conclusion and
findings as follows:

[12]      …You were well aware, Mr. Ahenakew,
that Mr. Parker was a reporter even if, as you testified, you could not
remember him from a previous person to person interview. You knew from the time
that he approached you and Vice-Chief Daniels that this was Mr. Parker of the
Star Phoenix who had written critical columns on First Nations affairs. You
knew that reporters do exactly what their job title describes, that is report.
They report what they personally see and hear and what other people tell them.
That was particularly true in the case of Mr. Parker, whose reputation was to
investigate and report First Nation issues in a critical manner.

[13]      Mr. Ahenakew, you also testified
that you had participated in approximately 1000 media interviews both by local
and national press. The defence attempted to make an issue of whether you were
aware that Mr. Parker had a tape recorder during the interview. In the opinion
of the court, it is irrelevant whether Mr. Parker had a tape recorder, a pencil
and a reporter’s note pad or simply intended to rely on his own recollection of
what was said during the interview. The tape recording simply adds to the
reliability of Mr. Parker’s recollection and recitation of the actual
interview. There is a substantial difference between a private conversation and
a interview, a difference that you, Mr. Ahenakew, from your experience with the
media, knew well. …

[
15
]  The trial judge concluded that some of the
statements made by Mr. Ahenakew during the interview, while being
“distortions, unbalanced opinions, bigoted outbursts and outright lies” did not
offend s. 319(2).  However, he found that other statements did meet the
required standard and convicted Mr. Ahenakew.  He fined Mr. Ahenakew $1000 and
gave him one year to pay.

V.     The Appeal Decision

[
16
]

Mr. Ahenakew appealed his
conviction.  His grounds of appeal included arguments that the trial judge had
erred in failing to find the interview with Mr. Parker to be a “private
conversation” and in failing to find that Mr. Ahenakew did not have the
mens
rea
required by s. 319(2).

[
17
]  The appeal judge found no error with respect to the
“private conversation” issue.  In a decision reported at
2006 SKQB 272
, (2006),
281 Sask. R. 47 he wrote this:

[20]      … The trial judge was entitled to
draw the inference he did from all of the surrounding circumstances, that the
appellant knew that his answers would be made public, and that he therefore
intended they be available to the public.  The trial judge did not err in his
interpretation of the word “private” in
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
,
nor did he err in law in concluding [Mr. Ahenakew’s] conversation with Mr.
Parker was not private.

[
18
]  However, with respect to the question of whether
Mr. Ahenakew had “wilfully” promoted hatred, the appeal judge found that the
trial judge had not referred to Mr. Ahenakew’s position nor considered all of
the relevant evidence.  The key aspect of his decision is reproduced below:

[31]      The theory of the defence that
emerges from the transcript of evidence on the issue of the appellant’s intent
with respect to the consequences of his words, and from the appellant’s
evidence, was that he spoke the words he did in anger in what he described as a
confrontation with Mr. Parker and that he did not have the intent to wilfully
promote hatred. There is uncontradicted evidence, apart from the appellant’s
evidence, relevant to this position.

[32]      Until Mr. Parker asked his first
question, the appellant had no knowledge about what the subject matter of the
questioning would be. Thereafter, his statements were made spontaneously in
response to questions from Mr. Parker. Mr. Parker agrees it was an
argumentative interview. In the course of the interview, the appellant stated, “Well,
I'm not gonna argue with you about the Jews”. At the end of the interview, the
appellant said, “Don't talk about them”, and walked away. Mr. Parker stated “Well
I wanted to keep the interview going. I had other questions but he had had
enough.”. The whole interview lasted approximately three minutes. When Mr.
Parker subsequently telephoned the appellant, the appellant hung up on him.

[33]      The foregoing evidence was relevant
on the issue of the appellant’s intent and his defence that he did not “wilfully
promote hatred of persons of the Jewish faith”. To the extent the foregoing
evidence, along with possible other evidence, was not taken into account by the
trial judge before drawing the inference he did was an error in law that
requires the setting aside of the judgment.

[
19
]  Mr. Ahenakew’s appeal was allowed, his conviction
quashed and a new trial ordered.

VI.   Analysis

[
20
]  In
R. v. Keegstra
, supra
, the Supreme Court
upheld the constitutional validity of
s. 319(2)
on the basis that it was a
reasonable limitation of the right of free speech guaranteed by s. 2(b) of the
Charter
.
In so doing, the Court noted that “wilfully” promoting hatred imported a
difficult burden for the Crown which would be satisfied only in circumstances
where an accused subjectively desired the promotion of hatred or foresaw such a
consequence as certain or substantially certain to result from the act done.
The Court also underlined the limited meaning of the word “promotes”.  Dickson
C.J.C. said this at pp. 776-777:

… Given the purpose of the provision to
criminalize the spreading of hatred in society, I find that the word “promotes”
indicates active support or instigation.  Indeed the French version of the
offence uses the verb “
fomenter
”, which in English means to foment or
stir up.  In “promotes” we thus have a word that indicates more than simple
encouragement or advancement.  The hate-monger must intend or foresee as
substantially certain a direct and active stimulation of hatred against an
identifiable group.

[
21
]  It is also well established
that, in considering a charge under
s. 319(2)
, a trial judge must consider not
only the words used by the accused, but the circumstances and context in which
they were spoken.  The Supreme Court commented as follows in
Mugesera v.
Canada

(Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)
,
2005 SCC 40
, [2005] 2 S.C.R.
100 at para.
106
:

106      As is the case with the crime of
incitement to genocide, the crime of incitement to hatred requires the trier of
fact to consider the speech objectively but with regard for the circumstances
in which the speech was given, the manner and tone used, and the persons to
whom the message was addressed.

[
22
]  The Crown’s appeal in this case must
be examined in light of that jurisprudential background. It is essential to
remember the restricted reach of
s. 319(2)
and to ensure that its
interpretation and application reflect not only the Supreme Court’s conclusions
about the pernicious nature of hate speech but that they also reflect the
Court’s obvious concerns about undue restrictions on freedom of expression.

[
23
]  Mr. Ahenakew says he did not “wilfully
promote” hatred.  He characterizes the interview with Mr. Parker as no more
than a short and angry confrontation precipitated by Mr. Parker himself.  Understandably,
he emphasizes the difference between the circumstances of the interview and the
situtations underpinning the leading cases in this area such as

R. v.
Keegstra
, supra
(an ongoing campaign aimed at students by a schoolteacher),

Mugesera v. Canada, supra
(a speech made to 1,000 people), and
R. v.
Buzzanga and Durocher
(1979),
1979 CanLII 1927 (ON CA)
, 49 C.C.C. (2d) 369 (Ont. C.A.) (distribution
of handbills).

[
24
]  Mr. Ahenakew says the following
evidence is relevant to the issue of intent:

(a)

Mr. Parker initiated the interview;

(b)

Mr. Ahenakew did not know the subject matter of the interview before it
started but expected it would be about the new consent forms required by the
Government;

(c)

The interview lasted only three minutes in total;

(d)

The overall tone of the
interview was abrupt and confrontational;

(e)

Most of Mr. Ahenakew’s statements were made in response to questions
from Mr. Parker;

(f)

Mr. Ahenakew’s statements were made only once and were not part of some
larger or ongoing initiative;

(g)

Midway through the interview, after being pressed by Mr. Parker
about his views, Mr. Ahenakew said “Well, I’m not gonna argue with you about
the Jews”;

(h)

Mr. Ahenakew ended the interview on his own initiative and walked away;

(i)

Mr. Parker desired to continue the interview and testified saying “Well,
I wanted to keep the interview going.  I had other questions, but he had had
enough”; and

(j)

Shortly after the interview, Mr. Parker phoned Mr. Ahenakew but Mr.
Ahenakew hung up on him.

[
25
]  The Crown quite properly does
not dispute that this evidence is relevant. However, it submits the decision of
the appeal judge was grounded on an incorrect legal premise.  It says he
wrongly assumed the trial judge was under a duty to provide reasons for
decision which laid out the theory of the defence and the evidence bearing on that
defence.  The Crown points, in particular, to the following passage from the
appeal judge’s reasons:

[27]      A trial judge’s obligation in a
criminal trial is to acknowledge and consider the positions and theories of
both the Crown and the defence in order to arrive at a proper appreciation of
the evidence. As noted per Cory J. in
R. v. G. (R.M.)
(1997),
1996 CanLII 176 (SCC)
, 110 C.C.C.
(3d) 26 at 32:

[9]        In the course of giving directions to a jury,
it is essential that the trial judge outline for them the theory or position of
the defence and refer the jury to the essential elements bearing on that
defence in such a way that it will ensure the jury’s proper appreciation of the
evidence ... [authorities omitted].

A trial judge sitting alone must instruct
himself or herself accordingly.

[
26
]  I agree that the appeal judge erred if he intended
to say a trial judge sitting alone commits an error of law if he or she
disposes of a case by way of reasons which do not set out the theory of the
defence and the evidence in the same way as would be expected of a judge
charging a jury. Judges sitting alone are under no such obligation.  The
Supreme Court made this clear in
R. v. Sheppard
,
2002 SCC 26
, [2002] 1
S.C.R. 869 where,  at p. 898, Binnie J. said “It is neither expected nor
required that the trial judge’s reasons provide the equivalent of a jury
instruction”.

[
27
]
Sheppard
holds that the adequacy of a trial
judge’s reasons is to be assessed from a functional perspective.  The lack of
reasons or the inadequacy of reasons, in and of itself, will be a basis for
overturning a trial decision only when, having regard to the particular circumstances
of the case, the reasons do not provide the basis for meaningful appellate
review of the trial decision. In
Sheppard
, Binnie J. elaborated on this
point as follows:

28        It is neither necessary nor
appropriate to limit circumstances in which an appellate court may consider
itself unable to exercise appellate review in a meaningful way.  The mandate of
the appellate court is to determine the correctness of the trial decision, and
a functional test requires that the trial judge's reasons be sufficient for
that purpose.  The appeal court itself is in the best position to make that
determination.  The threshold is clearly reached, as here, where the appeal
court considers itself unable to determine whether the decision is vitiated by
error…. The simple underlying rule is that if, in the opinion of the appeal
court, the deficiencies in the reasons prevent meaningful appellate review of
the correctness of the decision, then an error of law has been committed.

[
28
]  As the Supreme Court observed in
R. v. Braich
,

2002 SCC 27
, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 903 at paragraph
41
, “inadequate reasons” is not
an all-purpose ground of appeal that can serve to mask what is in fact a
disagreement between a trial judge and the members of an appeal court on an
issue which the law allocates to the trial court for decision.

[
29
]  All of that said, I do not accept the Crown’s
characterization of the appeal judge’s decision.  Specifically, I do not read
his decision as suggesting merely that the trial judge erred by failing to
produce reasons which referenced all of the evidence bearing on the
mens rea

aspect of the offence created by
s. 319(2)
.  I understand his decision to say
that, taken as a whole, the trial judge’s reasons reveal, in positive terms, a
failure to consider relevant evidence.  In other words, the appeal judge did
not find the quality of the trial judge’s reasons, in and of itself, to be the basis
for overturning the conviction. Rather, he found that the reasons disclosed a
substantive error of law in the form of a failure to consider relevant
evidence.

[
30
]  This is the sort of approach taken by Laskin C.J.C.
in
Macdonald v. The Queen
,
1976 CanLII 140 (SCC)
, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665.  In that case, he
expressed reservations about imposing a general duty on judges to give reasons
but, nonetheless, said at p. 673:

It does not follow, however, that
failure of a trial judge to give reasons, not challengeable
per se
as an
error of law, will be equally unchallengeable if, having regard to the record,
there is a rational basis for concluding that the trial judge erred in
appreciation of a relevant issue or in appreciation of evidence that would
affect the propriety of his verdict.

[
31
]  The Supreme Court’s decision in
Harper v. The
Queen
,
1982 CanLII 11 (SCC)
, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 2 is to a similar effect.  The Court in that case
concluded the trial court had “fatally overlooked” relevant defence evidence.
Estey J. said this at p. 14:

… Where the record, including the reasons for judgment,
discloses a lack of appreciation of relevant evidence and more particularly the
complete disregard of such evidence, then it falls upon the reviewing tribunal
to intercede.

[
32
]  Both
Macdonald
and
Harper
were
referred to in
Sheppard
with apparent approval.

[
33
]  The key point is this.
Sheppard
does not
displace the fundamental proposition that a trial judge must have regard to all
of the relevant evidence when determining the guilt of an accused person.  If a
trial judge’s reasons reveal a failure to consider such evidence, as opposed to
a mere failure to record it, the decision of the judge will have been made on
the basis of an error of law.  Accordingly, notwithstanding his perhaps
unfortunate reference to
R. v. G.(R.M.)
, I see no problem in principle
with the basic approach taken by the appeal judge.  The trial judge did err if
he failed to consider evidence bearing on the issue of intent.

[
34
]  I turn, therefore, to the facts at hand.  In my
view, there are two aspects of the trial judge’s reasons which, taken together,
demonstrate in positive terms that he did not consider all of the relevant evidence
concerning intent.

[
35
]  The first relates to the overall structure of his
reasons.  As noted above, the trial judge began his analysis of the case by
turning to the comments Mr. Ahenakew made during his speech.  In analyzing
those comments, the trial judge quoted the relevant passages in full.  He
referred to the length of the speech, noted it was wide-ranging and observed
that it was riddled with profanity.  He also noted that the speech was made
over a public address system and was videotaped.  Earlier in his reasons, he
had recounted further context by referencing Mr. Ahenakew’s prominence as a
First Nations politician and the fact he had been invited to attend the
conference to speak.

[
36
]  The trial judge concluded his assessment of Mr.
Ahenakew’s speech by saying he was left with a reasonable doubt as to
Mr. Ahenakew’s guilt in light of “… the nature of [his] presentation, its
lack of focus and the slight possibility that [he] did not intend by [his]
statements to foster hatred against Jews.”

[
37
]  The judge next turned to the interview and quoted
it in full. He then examined the question of whether the interview was a “private
conversation” between Mr. Ahenakew and Mr. Parker.  He considered this issue by
referring expressly to the relevant evidence and context.  This included Mr. Ahenakew’s
testimony to the effect that he knew Mr. Parker was a reporter and that he had
had considerable experience with reporters and understood their role.  The
trial judge quoted a key passage from the transcript and then dealt
specifically with Mr. Ahenakew’s characterization of the interview as a
confrontation following an “ambush” by Mr. Parker.

[
38
]  Having found that the interview was not a private
conversation, the trial judge moved on to consider the question of “wilful
promotion of hatred.”  He proceeded, as I read his reasons, by first examining
in detail the issue of whether various parts of Mr. Ahenakew’s comments during
the interview involved “hatred.”  This led him to identify six of the least
offensive comments made by Mr. Ahenakew and, in relation to them, to find that “the
Crown has failed to discharge the onus of proving beyond a reasonable doubt
that [Mr. Ahenakew] did wilfully promote hatred against people of the Jewish
faith.”

[
39
]  He next quoted three statements by Mr. Ahenakew
which he said did meet “the stringent requirement of
section 319(2)
.”  They are
set out below:

1.

You know, how, how do you get rid of a, a, a,
disease like that that’s gonna take over, that’s gonna dominate, that’s gonna
everything and the poor people, they …

2.

That’s why he fried six million of those guys,
you know.

3.

Parker:       But to liberate the world from
dictatorship that was killing people           killing Jews, killing Jews,
killing gypsies, killing homosexuals,                killing all sorts of
people.

Ahenakew:  Exactly, wanna clean up the world.  I, I don’t support Hitler but I

Parker:        That’s what it sounds
like.

Ahenakew:  Well, you know, he cleaned up a hell of a lot of
things, didn’t he? You’d be dominated by, you’d be owned by the Jews right now
the world over.

[
40
]  I observe, parenthetically, that the parties did
not make any submissions about the trial judge’s decision to focus only on
three features of the interview as opposed to considering the interview in its
entirety.  As a result, I make no comment, one way or the other, about the
propriety of that approach.

[
41
]  In relation to the three statements he identified,
the trial judge said only this:

[21]      When one hears the audio tape and
the fury and passion in the delivery of these statements, the court is
convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that the sole purpose and intent in making
these statements was to wilfully promote hatred against people of the Jewish
faith within the meaning of section 319 (2) of the
Act.
To equate a
definable group of people to a disease is to dehumanize them, to deny them the
basic respect and dignity that all human beings are entitled to and that it is
justified to kill or to use the more offensive word, “fried”, is clearly to
subject them to being despised and subject to ill treatment even in the extreme
such as was demonstrated by the Holocaust. Daily Canadians and our Governments
are being urged to eradicate diseases such as cancer, aids, tuberculosis - to
suggest that any human being or a group of human beings are a disease is to
invite extremists to take action and to give a justification for violence
against them. This is precisely why Parliament enacted section 319 (2) and our
Supreme Court of Canada declared it as being constitutional.

[22]      Similarly, I totally reject your
testimony that your comments on December 13, 2002 were prompted or affected by
diabetes, wine or change in medication. Your appearance, demeanor and delivery
belie that defence.

[23]      Accordingly, I find you, David
Ahenakew, guilty of wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group to
wit people of the Jewish faith contrary to
section 319 (2)
of the
Criminal
Code of Canada
.

[
42
]  The noteworthy feature of paragraph 21 is that, in
it, the trial judge referred only to the fury and passion in Mr. Ahenakew’s
delivery as factors bearing on the question of whether he had “wilfully
promoted” hatred. When compared to how he structured the balance of his
reasons, the content of paragraph 21 suggests that these were the only factors
he took into consideration.  I say this because, in relation to each of the
other aspects of his analysis, the trial judge laid out or referred to all of
the significant evidence relevant to the issue he was examining.  He took this
approach in relation to Mr. Ahenakew’s speech, in relation to the “private
conversation” question and in relation to the issue of “hatred.”  In light of
all that, it would be unusual if, when considering “wilful promotion,” the
trial judge changed his approach and, for the first and only time, decided to
refer to only a small part of the evidence bearing on the problem before him.  Rather,
it can be expected that, as with the rest of his reasons, he adverted directly
to the whole of the relevant evidence. I observe here, as well, that the trial
judge, in paragraph 22, mentioned Mr. Ahenakew’s diabetes, his consumption of
wine and the fact he was on medication.  This too is consistent with his
approach of at least mentioning all of the evidence seen as being relevant to
the issues before him.

[
43
]  Accordingly, the overall structure of the trial
judge’s reasons indicates not merely that he did not mention evidence relevant
to whether Mr. Ahenakew wilfully promoted hatred.  When compared to the
rest of his reasons, the failure to note the nature and context of the Parker interview
reveals that he simply did not take the evidence on those matters into account.

[
44
]  The second point of importance here is that the
trial judge
did
mention some of the key evidence going to intent but took
that step only in the context of dealing with the “private conversation”
issue.  As part of his consideration of whether the interview was private, he
said this:

[14]      Mr. Ahenakew, you are a
self-described First Nations politician. Defence evidence called by your
counsel indicates that during your leadership of First Nations in Canada you have engaged in rough and tumble
politics. You can hardly maintain that you were taken off guard by the
questions posed by Mr. Parker nor can the court put any weight in your
description of the conversation as that being a confrontation or that you were
somehow the subject of an ambush interview by Mr. Parker. Nothing in the video
of your speech to the conference, nor in the audio recording of your interview
with Mr. Parker indicates you being timid, unsure or rattled. Indeed, your
demeanor bordered on self-confidence to the point of arrogance.

[
45
]  Not insignificantly, these comments track the
arguments on the issue of intent that were advanced at the end of the trial.
Mr. Ahenakew’s counsel had made this submission:

I will quickly move then to the other issue
and say a few words about that.  Intent is, of course, specific.  What I mean
by that is
it’s not enough to intend the expression of hatred, it is
necessary to intend the promotion of hatred. … A very heated exchange, quickly
in about five minutes.  It’s really wrong to infer much from that
… But
they got the hot button they wanted -- he, that is Mr. Parker, wanted the best
story of his life.  It was only possible when he got an answer to the single
question on tape, do you believe it.  From that point on we have a conversation
of -- oh, I really wish I’d measured the time because I doubt that it’s five
minutes, in which
there’s a heated exchange and statements are made that
David Ahenakew did not think about, had not intended to talk about, hadn’t
planned and when they became known he realized he had made a mistake
… So
having apologized as abjectly as he did, having had no premeditation in his
statement, having said it once, on one occasion, never having consented to it,
never
having thought about it in advance and not even thinking about it at the time,
constantly being interrupted, and I say bated in an ambush interview
, this
is the clearest case… [Emphasis added]

[
46
]  In my view, the trial judge’s mention of this evidence
in the context of the “private conversation” aspect of
s. 319(2)
, but not in
the context of the “wilful promotion of hatred” point, indicates that he did
not consider it in relation to the latter issue.

[
47
]  As a consequence, I conclude the trial judge erred
in law, not because he failed to set out in his reasons all of the evidence
concerning intent, but because his reasons reveal he did not take relevant
evidence into account.  In the result, I see no mistake in the conclusion of
the appeal judge.

[
48
]  I do wish, however, to add a qualification to the analysis
of the appeal judge.  As I read his decision, particularly at paragraph 28, he
appears to have proceeded on the basis that the trial judge did not consider
evidence relevant to the issue of the “wilfulness” aspect of the offence under

s. 319(2)
.  However, as I understand Mr. Ahenakew’s position, he says the
nature of the interview and the circumstances surrounding it also establish
that he did not “promote”

hatred.  In other words, he draws a
distinction between promoting hatred and simply making hateful comments.  The
theory of this aspect of the defence thereby picks up the Supreme Court’s
comments in
Keegstra
,
supra
, about the restricted meaning of
“promotes”.

[
49
]  Accordingly, if this matter is re-tried, I would
not want this decision to be interpreted as meaning Mr. Ahenakew’s characterization
of the interview is relevant only to the notion of whether he “wilfully”
promoted hatred.  It is also relevant to the question of whether he “promoted”
hatred.

[
50
]  As a final point, I also note that the Crown submits
Mr. Ahenakew admitted having the intent necessary for a conviction under
s.
319(2)
.   It points to a passage from his testimony at trial where his counsel
asked him to comment on the aspect of the Parker interview where Mr. Ahenakew
had said “that’s – how Hitler came in, he was going to make damn sure that the
Jews didn’t take over Germany or Europe, that’s why he fried six million of
those guys, you know”.  The specific part of the transcript relied on by the
Crown reads as follows:

Q         -- is that what you believed?

A         Because of what I heard, that’s what I believed, yes.  I
never -- never spoke to the Jews, even when I was in Israel, Egypt and so on.

Q         Would you have said those things in a public forum if they
were going to be broadcast to the world?

A         No, because everybody knows - - I know that would be
classified as hate.  Hate mongering or - - I wouldn’t do that to any people.

Q         Even though you might believe it?

A         Yes, because it is a destructive - - destructive event
that took place over there.

[
51
]  The prosecutor did not place any special emphasis
on this evidence in his submissions at trial.  Neither the trial judge nor the
appeal judge made reference to it in their decisions.  I too fail to see that
it has the significance now suggested by the Crown.  Indeed, in my view, Mr.
Ahenakew’s statements are open to being read as undercutting the Crown’s case.
In other words, they could be read as meaning that Mr. Ahenakew did
not

intend to foment or stir up hatred. In any event, there is nothing in Mr.
Ahenakew’s words which acknowledges that, in speaking with Mr. Parker, he
wilfully promoted hatred within the specific and limited meaning of those terms
as defined in
R. v. Keegstra
,
supra
.

VII.  Conclusion

[
52
]  Mr. Ahenakew’s comments, on any
standard, were shocking, brutal and hurtful.  However, that is not the measure
of the offence prescribed by
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
.  It engages
only in circumstances where a person “wilfully promotes” hatred against an
identifiable group.  I agree with the appeal judge that, at trial, there was a
failure to consider all of the evidence relevant to the question of whether Mr. Ahenakew
had the intent necessary for a finding of guilt.

[
53
]  Leave to appeal is granted but the Crown’s appeal
is dismissed.
